id: Daily Trials by a Sensitive Man

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Oh, there are times When all this fret and tumult that we hear Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear His own dull chimes. Ding dong! ding dong! The world is in a simmer like a sea Over a pent volcano,—woe is me All the day long! From crib to shroud! Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby, And friends in boots tramp round us as we die, Snuffling aloud. At morning’s call The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun, And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one, Give answer all. When evening dim Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul, Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,— These are our hymn. Women, with tongues Like polar needles, ever on the jar; Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are Within their lungs. Children, with drums Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass; Peripatetics with a blade of grass Between their thumbs. Vagrants, whose arts Have caged some devil in their mad machine, Which grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between, Come out by starts. Cockneys that kill Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams, Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams From hill to hill. Soldiers, with guns, Making a nuisance of the blessed air, Child-crying bellman, children in despair, Screeching for buns. Storms, thunders, waves! Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill; Ye sometimes rest; men never can be still But in their graves.

outputs.L1:
Oh, there are times when all this fret and tumult that we hear  
Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear  
His own dull chimes.

Ding-dong! Ding-dong!  
The world is in a simmer, like a sea  
Above a pent volcano—woe is me!—  
All the day long.

From crib to shroud,  
Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby,  
And friends in boots tramp round us as we die,  
Snuffling aloud.

At morning’s call,  
The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun,  
And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one,  
Give answer all.

When evening dim  
Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul—  
Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall—  
These are our hymn.

Women, with tongues  
Like polar needles, ever on the jar;  
Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are  
Within their lungs.

Children, with drums  
Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass;  
Peripatetics with a blade of grass  
Between their thumbs.

Vagrants, whose arts  
Have caged some devil in their mad machine,  
Which, grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between  
That issue forth by starts.

Cockneys who kill  
Thin horses of a Sunday; men with clams,  
Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams  
From hill to hill.

Soldiers, with guns,  
Making a nuisance of the blessed air;  
Child-crying bellmen; children in despair,  
Screeching for buns.

Storms, thunders, waves!  
Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill;  
Ye sometimes rest—men never can be still  
But in their graves.
outputs.L2:
At moments, the endless agitation and noise around us grow even more tiresome than a gravedigger finds the monotonous ringing of his own bells: ding-dong, ding-dong. The world seethes like an ocean covering a trapped volcano, and its uproar torments me from morning to night.

Noise follows us from cradle to coffin. Nurses shriek songs over us as infants, while, at the end of life, booted friends stomp about our deathbeds and sniff loudly.

At daybreak, a yapping pug greets the sunrise. Then flea-ridden mixed-breed dogs wake in succession and answer its call.

As twilight closes in, solitary cats begin their harsh wailing. One gives a sharp solo, two produce a bitter duet, and soon all join in a universal screech—our evening hymn.

Women possess tongues that, like compass needles pointing north, are always quivering and clattering. Men are uncorked fountains of words, with the source of their endless flow buried deep in their lungs.

Children carry drums fastened to them by foolishly indulgent fathers. Wandering pedestrians whistle through blades of grass held between their thumbs.

Vagrants operate crazed contraptions in which they seem to have imprisoned a demon. As the machines grind, they release squeals in sudden bursts, interrupted by rough, groaning sounds.

London townsmen drive worn-out horses to exhaustion on Sundays. Other men sell clams with cries as hoarse as young bison calling across the hills for their mothers.

Soldiers foul the blessed air with gunfire. Bellmen shout like crying children, while genuinely miserable children scream for buns.

So let storms, thunder, and waves howl, smash, and roar as much as they please. Even they eventually fall quiet; human beings, however, remain noisy until they lie in their graves.
outputs.L3:
The speaker portrays the world’s unending noise and turmoil as stale, oppressive, and impossible to escape. From birth until death, human beings are surrounded by an exhausting clamor that penetrates every aspect of daily life. Animals add to the disturbance through the barking of dogs and the caterwauling of cats, while men, women, and children contribute with incessant conversation, cries, drums, whistles, and other jarring sounds.

The streets are equally chaotic. Performers, travelers, soldiers, bellmen, and other city dwellers fill the air with shouts, gunfire, mechanical squeaks, and countless additional disturbances. Together, these noises create a relentless atmosphere of disorder that leaves the speaker weary and disillusioned.

Natural sounds may be violent, but they are temporary: storms pass, thunder fades, and waves eventually grow calm. Human noise, by contrast, seems endless. In the speaker’s bleak view, true silence can be found only in the grave.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents human existence as an unbroken succession of sounds. From the cries that accompany birth to the ceremonies surrounding death, life is portrayed as crowded with voices, arguments, laughter, music, work, and mechanical clatter. The speaker builds this impression through a long catalogue of noisy people, animals, machines, instruments, and natural forces. Each new example adds to the sense that silence is constantly being invaded and that no part of the world remains untouched by commotion.

This accumulation creates much of the poem’s satire. Human beings appear incapable of living quietly: they shout, quarrel, celebrate, labor, preach, perform, and compete to make themselves heard. The sounds of animals, vehicles, tools, and music join their voices, turning society into a vast, disorderly chorus. Even noises that might ordinarily seem pleasant or meaningful become tiring when placed within this relentless sequence. Through exaggeration and repetition, the poem transforms everyday sound into evidence of humanity’s restless and exhausting nature.

Natural forces also contribute to the uproar. Wind, thunder, storms, and the sea seem powerful enough to continue forever, yet even they eventually subside. The storm passes, the waves grow calm, and the natural world recovers its stillness. Humanity, however, is granted no comparable peace during life. Social activity continues without pause, and one form of noise is immediately replaced by another.

The poem therefore ends on a darkly comic and sobering conclusion: true quiet comes to human beings only in the grave. Death alone offers escape from the ceaseless demands and disturbances of society. By contrasting nature’s temporary turbulence with humanity’s lifelong commotion, the poem emphasizes the inescapability of noise and presents silence not as an ordinary comfort, but as a final condition beyond life.
outputs.L5:
**When His Ding Changed Everything**

When the old clock gave its final ding, Elias looked up from his book. His grandfather had warned him that, one day, the clock would stop—and when it did, a hidden door would open.

Behind the clock, the wall slowly shifted.

Elias smiled, reached for his lantern, and stepped toward the darkness. His adventure had begun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.’s poem “The Music-Grinders” in full.
counterfactuals.output:
## “The Music-Grinders”  
*Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.*

There are three ways in which men take  
One’s money from his purse,  
And very hard it is to tell  
Which of the three is worse;  
But all of them are bad enough  
To make a body curse.

You’re riding out some pleasant day,  
And counting up your gains;  
A fellow jumps from out a bush,  
And takes your horse’s reins,  
Another hints some words about  
A bullet in your brains.

It’s hard to meet such pressing friends,  
In such a lonely spot;  
It’s very hard to lose your cash,  
But harder to be shot;  
And so you take your wallet out,  
Though you would rather not.

Perhaps you’re going out to dine,—  
Some filthy creature begs  
You’ll hear about the cannon-ball  
That carried off his pegs,  
And says it is a dreadful thing  
For men to lose their legs.

He tells you of his starving wife,  
His children to be fed,  
Poor little, lovely innocents,  
All clamorous for bread,—  
And so you kindly help to put  
A bachelor to bed.

You’re sitting on your window-seat,  
Beneath a cloudless moon;  
You hear a sound, that seems to wear  
The semblance of a tune,  
As if a broken fife should strive  
To drown a cracked bassoon.

And nearer, nearer still, the tide  
Of music seems to come,  
There’s something like a human voice,  
And something like a drum;  
You sit in speechless agony,  
Until your ear is numb.

Poor “Home, Sweet Home!” should seem to be  
A very dismal place;  
Your “Auld Acquaintance,” all at once,  
Is altered in the face;  
Their discords sting through Burns and Moore,  
Like hedgehogs dressed in lace.

You think they are crusaders, sent  
From some infernal clime,  
To pluck the eyes of Sentiment  
And dock the tail of Rhyme,  
To crack the voice of Melody  
And break the legs of Time.

But, hark! the air again is still,  
The music all is ground,  
And silence, like a poultice, comes  
To heal the blows of sound;  
It cannot be—it is—it is—  
A hat is going round!

No! Pay the dentist when he leaves  
A fracture in your jaw,  
And pay the owner of the bear  
That stunned you with his paw,  
And buy the lobster that has had  
Your knuckles in his claw;

But if you are a portly man,  
Put on your fiercest frown,  
And talk about a constable  
To turn them out of town;  
Then close your sentence with an oath,  
And shut the window down!

And if you are a slender man,  
Not big enough for that,  
Or, if you cannot make a speech,  
Because you are a flat,  
Go very quietly and drop  
A button in the hat!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Find and reproduce the nineteenth-century poem containing the lines “The world is in a simmer like a sea / Over a pent volcano.”
counterfactuals.output:
The lines are from **_A Life-Drama_ (1853)** by the Scottish poet **Alexander Smith (1829–1867)**:

> The world is in a simmer, like a sea  
> Over a pent volcano.

_A Life-Drama_ is not a short lyric but a book-length dramatic poem, running to several thousand lines; consequently, reproducing the entire work in one response would be impractical. It is sometimes catalogued under the expanded title **_A Life-Drama and Other Poems_**, the collection in which it first appeared.
